reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A smoking-related disease of young to middle-aged adults; almost all patients are current or former smokers.
Presents with cough and breathlessness, and up to a quarter present with spontaneous pneumothorax; constitutional symptoms may also occur.
The HRCT hallmark is a combination of nodules, which cavitate, and bizarrely shaped thick-walled cysts, with upper- and mid-zone predominance and sparing of the costophrenic angles.
Early disease is nodular and evolves to a predominantly cystic pattern over time.
Histology shows bronchiolocentric stellate nodules of Langerhans cells that are CD1a and S100 positive, with Birbeck granules on electron microscopy and admixed eosinophils.
BRAF V600E and other activating MAPK-pathway mutations are found in a substantial proportion, supporting a clonal neoplastic basis.
Smoking cessation is essential and can lead to regression; progressive disease may require systemic therapy.
Pulmonary hypertension is a recognised and prognostically important complication.
reference.pathophysiology: Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis involves accumulation and proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that form bronchiolocentric granulomatous nodules, driven by tobacco smoke exposure in clonally susceptible individuals who frequently harbour activating MAPK-pathway mutations such as BRAF V600E. Nodules undergo cavitation and cystic transformation to produce the characteristic nodulocystic upper-zone disease and, over time, fibrosis and pulmonary vascular remodelling.
additionalDifferentials: Respiratory bronchiolitis-ILD and desquamative interstitial pneumonia
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax demonstrating nodules and cysts with upper- and mid-zone predominance
Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor, often showing a reduced gas transfer with obstructive, restrictive or mixed defects
Bronchoalveolar lavage with increased CD1a-positive cells as supportive evidence
Lung biopsy with CD1a and S100 immunostaining where the diagnosis is unclear
BRAF mutation testing in progressive or multisystem disease
Echocardiography and, where indicated, right heart catheterisation for pulmonary hypertension
redFlags: Signs of pulmonary hypertension or right heart failure
Multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with diabetes insipidus, bone lesions or skin involvement
reference.prognosis: The course is variable; many patients stabilise or improve with smoking cessation, but a subset progresses to cystic destruction, fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension and respiratory failure, with pulmonary hypertension worsening the outlook.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the disease in a lifelong non-smoker without reconsideration
Mistaking cysts for emphysema or lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Not testing for BRAF mutations in progressive or multisystem disease
Failing to screen for pulmonary hypertension and underestimating the risk of recurrent pneumothorax
